source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning
finding: On 108 SyGuS text-editing problems, learning a library raised the solve rate from near zero to near the best hand-built solver.
numbers: Before learning: 3.7% solved in 10 min, mean search 235 s. After learning: 79.6%, mean 40 s. CVC4 (1 h, 8 CPUs, hand-made library per problem): 82.4%. DreamCoder with the same large budget: 84.3%. Trained on 128 tasks, tested on 108.
limits: Text editing is a domain with clean reuse. The CVC4 comparison uses a different budget from the 10 min setting.
agent_relevance: Best case for a memory of solved subgoals: big gain when tasks share structure and checks are exact.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning
finding: Ablations and baselines across six domains: both the library (compression) and the recognition model (dreaming) were needed. Memorise-the-solution baselines did worse than compression.
numbers: Held-out accuracy over 20 wake/sleep cycles, 5 runs, error bars 1 sd. In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative model solved more than 60% of held-out tasks; DreamCoder reached nearly 100%. Mean solve time 54.1 s (median 15.0 s). Training to convergence about a day on 20 to 100 CPUs.
quote: each of DreamCoder's core components ... contributes substantively to its overall performance
limits: Exact per-ablation numbers are in figures and the supplement, not the main text. Domains were chosen where library learning works. Each domain starts from a hand-built core of control flow, higher-order functions and types.
agent_relevance: Storing raw solutions (memorise) is not enough. What helps is a shorter reusable form plus a guide for when to use it.

source: Ellis et al. (2021) DreamCoder: bootstrapping inductive program synthesis with wake-sleep library learning
finding: Larger, deeper libraries go with more tasks solved. Learning from a minimal base is very costly. Poor abstractions are said to widen search.
numbers: Learning 20 recursion tasks from 1959-Lisp primitives took about 5 days on 64 CPUs (rediscovered fold, unfold, map, zip). Physics: 93% of 60 laws solved after 8 cycles. Authors say the origami basis took about a year of total CPU time.
limits: Cost is large when learning from scratch. The authors themselves chose to build in generic primitives instead.
agent_relevance: A library is a fixed up-front price; it pays only if reuse is frequent. Count setup cost (our G7).

source: Wong et al. (2021) LAPS: Leveraging language to learn program abstractions and search heuristics
finding: Adding language descriptions to DreamCoder gave better libraries, and the gain held even with no language at test time.
numbers: Held-out % solved, synthetic language. Strings (n=500): DreamCoder 33.4, LAPS neural search 52.2, +mutual exclusivity 57.0, +language-program compression 54.6. Graphics (n=111), best/mean over seeds: DreamCoder 49.55/42.64; LAPS+ME 86.49/80.18; LAPS+ME+compression 98.19/81.98. Scenes (n=115): DreamCoder 67.8 curriculum / 73.9 mean; LAPS 95.6 / 95.9. No language at test, enumeration from the library alone, Graphics: DreamCoder library 41.44, LAPS library 62.16.
quote: Adding poor abstractions can actually be detrimental: they increase the combinatorial search space.
limits: Large spread between best and mean seed in graphics (98.19 vs 81.98), so single runs overstate. Human-language train and test on strings: 48.6, below synthetic 54.6. Synthetic annotations come from templates.
agent_relevance: Names and descriptions help choose what to store, and the gain survives without the text. Store a plain-language description with each item.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: LILO (LLM writes programs, Stitch compresses, LLM documents) beat DreamCoder in all three domains on online synthesis, most in LOGO and REGEX. Most of the REGEX gain came from the plain LLM solver, not the library.
numbers: Held-out mean over runs (max). REGEX: DreamCoder 43.93 (45.6), LLM Solver 76.13 (90.0), LILO 77.07 (93.2), std 14.14. CLEVR: DreamCoder 94.50, LLM Solver 88.67, LILO 96.76. LOGO: DreamCoder 28.53, LLM Solver 32.13, LILO 48.95 (max 73.87), std 22.15. LILO minus DreamCoder: +33.14 REGEX, +2.26 CLEVR, +20.42 LOGO. LILO minus LLM Solver: +0.94, +8.09, +16.82.
limits: Run-to-run spread is very large (std 14 and 22 points). On REGEX the LLM solver with no library already gains +32.2 over DreamCoder. GPT models only.
agent_relevance: Check the library's own contribution apart from the LLM search; in REGEX it was under 1 point.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Giving the LLM compressed but unnamed abstractions made it worse. Auto-documentation (names plus descriptions) repaired part of the loss.
numbers: Change vs LLM Solver after Stitch compression with no docs: -30.60 REGEX, -2.91 CLEVR, -11.11 LOGO. Adding AutoDoc: +9.73 REGEX, +2.27 CLEVR, +0.00 LOGO over the undocumented condition.
quote: GPT struggled to deploy anonymous abstractions in contextually-appropriate ways
limits: In LOGO the documentation did not help because some descriptions were wrong (semantic errors); the docs come from GPT, which can misread code.
agent_relevance: A stored skill without a readable name and purpose can hurt a language model. Check that a description matches behaviour before storing (G2, G3).

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: An LLM asked to do the compression step itself failed: few valid outputs and almost no compression.
numbers: Only 19.01% (998 of 5250) of generated abstractions were valid: REGEX 24.93%, CLEVR 24.20%, LOGO 4.93%. Compression hovered near 1.0x. Stitch gave longer abstractions; GPT-4 gave trivial ones.
limits: GPT-4 with one prompt design, tested offline; the authors did not run the full online loop with it.
agent_relevance: Do compression with code, not the model (G5). The model should only name and explain.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Libraries built inside the loop worked better than libraries built after the fact, and they worked with no language at test time.
numbers: Offline synthesis from the final library, no language, gain over the base language: DreamCoder library +19.6 REGEX, +62.46 CLEVR, +29.73 LOGO; LILO library +42.27, +63.43, +43.24.
limits: Offline test uses enumerative search, so it measures the library alone (a good design). Three domains, each with a hand-built base language.
agent_relevance: Test library quality apart from the model: run a fixed searcher with and without the library. We should do this.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: LLM search cost about the same as enumerative search at the time.
numbers: One LILO training iteration is about equal to an 1800 s enumerative search on 96 CPUs (about 48 CPU-hours). Dollar cost per iteration: REGEX 1.16 (DreamCoder 1.16), CLEVR 0.71, LOGO 2.07. Domains with short timeouts (CLEVR) were 2 to 2.5x cheaper by enumeration.
limits: Prices change; the authors say the result depends on market factors.
agent_relevance: Cost parity means gains must be judged at equal spend (G7).

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: Stitch matched or beat DreamCoder's compression and was far faster and lighter.
numbers: 3 to 4 orders of magnitude faster and more than 2 orders less memory; Stitch single-thread, DreamCoder on 8 CPUs; tens of milliseconds per library in five domains. In the list domain Stitch compressed better more often than not but sometimes lost.
limits: Metric is compression, not solved tasks. Stitch alone misses some higher-order abstractions that DreamCoder finds.
agent_relevance: Compression can be done by cheap code, so the model need not do it.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: On large graphics corpora DreamCoder could not run at all. Stitch did.
numbers: Eight domains from Wong et al. 2022, 50 random 80/20 splits. Test compression ratio: nuts&bolts 11.57, houses 8.85, furniture 4.85, vehicles 4.14, gadgets 3.91, bridges 3.78, cities 3.06, castles 2.55. Runtime 0.24 to 77.26 s; peak memory 11 to 684 MB. DreamCoder found no abstraction with hours and 256 GB RAM, even after subsampling.
limits: No baseline comparison is possible; compression is not task accuracy.
agent_relevance: Compression held on held-out programs (train 12.00 vs test 11.57 in nuts&bolts), a sign of real reuse and not overfitting.

source: Bowers et al. (2023) Top-down synthesis for library learning (Stitch)
finding: Pruning rules are what make it scale. Combined with a deductive step, it recovers DreamCoder's core higher-order functions at a small fraction of the compute.
numbers: Ablations ran under 50 GB and 90 min. Removing argument-capture pruning hit the memory limit on more than half the domains. Removing redundant-argument pruning gave about 2x slowdown in the bridge domain. DreamCoder with 4 rewrite steps: about 2.5 days; pyStitch under 1 hour, using under 2% of its compute, only when version spaces and Bayesian re-ranking were both added.
limits: Method paper, from the DreamCoder group. Without the extras it missed some higher-order functions.
agent_relevance: An anytime, cost-bounded compressor suits a scaffold with a token budget.

source: Cao et al. (2023) babble: Learning better abstractions with e-graphs and anti-unification
finding: Library learning that handles equivalent rewrites (e-graphs) gave better compression than DreamCoder in far less time, on DreamCoder's own benchmarks.
numbers: Reported better compression orders of magnitude faster. Benchmarks: list, physics, text and logo domains from DreamCoder, plus the 2d CAD corpus that DreamCoder cannot run. Babble on one core, DreamCoder on 8 cores.
limits: I read the abstract, setup and plots; per-domain ratios are in figures only. Compression, not accuracy. Needs a hand-written equational theory per domain.
agent_relevance: Domain rewrite rules (symmetries) help the compressor; links to our G3 use of symmetries as checks.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: Helper functions refactored from about 200 examples raised accuracy for many LLM agents, but the gain was uneven across models and domains, and sometimes negative.
numbers: Accuracy, 3 seeds, primitives vs ReGAL. LOGO: CodeLlama-13B 45.6 to 57.1; CodeLlama-7B 34.5 to 34.5 (no change); GPT-3.5 36.9 to 49.3. Date: 13B 42.8 to 68.9; GPT-3.5 88.9 to 90.2. TextCraft: 13B 18.8 to 26.9; 34B 22.2 to 30.8. MATH algebra: GPT-3.5 43.2 to 55.4; Lemur-70B 14.0 to 13.1 (lower). TabMWP: 13B 29.1 to 27.9 and Lemur-70B 27.5 to 25.7 (lower).
limits: Gains shrink as the base model gets strong (Date, GPT-3.5: +1.3). The 7B and 13B MATH cells with ReGAL are both 17.6, which looks like a typo. The baseline uses the same retrieved examples, a fair control.
agent_relevance: Library gain is largest for weaker models and domains with obvious sub-shapes. For a strong model it can be near zero. Test per model.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: Each ReGAL component mattered. Curriculum (short to long) and retrying failed refactors mattered most.
numbers: CodeLlama-13B, dev splits. Full: LOGO 55.0, Date 77.0, TextCraft 34.12. No retry: 48.3, 51.9, 30.43. No curriculum: 36.3, 56.6, 28.78 (18.7 point drop on LOGO). No pruning: 52.0, 65.5, 25.26. No editing: 53.3, 69.6, 27.35.
limits: Dev set, one model. Curriculum uses average token length as a proxy for difficulty.
agent_relevance: Order tasks easy to hard, verify each stored helper by running it, and prune helpers that fail (G2).

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: With fewer examples and under distribution shift, the gains persisted but were small. Pruning and updating the library on new data added more.
numbers: TextCraft, 13B: +2.56 points with 25 demonstrations, +8.45 with about half the data. Under shift to unseen objects: primitives 7.8, ReGAL 11.4; plus pruning on unseen dev 14.9; plus all stages 17.2 (9.4 over baseline).
limits: Absolute accuracies are low (under 20%). Authors note some domains have no reusable abstraction and the primitives may already form a good language.
agent_relevance: A library needs upkeep: prune what fails on new tasks (links to no-goods).

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad, Bansal (2024) ReGAL: Refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: Reuse was shown by counting calls to the top helpers; error analysis credited both reuse and simpler reasoning.
numbers: Top-5 helper call counts shown per dataset (most relative reuse in TextCraft). On 25 LOGO cases only the ReGAL agent got right, the baseline mostly erred on angles or on using embed().
limits: Counting top-5 calls does not separate reuse from 'a verified example in the prompt'. Later papers (b20 to b25) raise exactly this.
agent_relevance: Two mechanisms are mixed: reuse and decomposition. Accuracy alone cannot tell which gave the gain.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: Inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes
finding: Letting the model induce a toolbox and trimming rarely used tools raised accuracy over primitive-only, and an always-add baseline (INSTANCE) did worse.
numbers: CodeLlama-7B: correctness up 30 to 120% (relative) over primitive-only across 7 math sets; 8.7 to 83.3% over INSTANCE with 60.0 to 90.2% fewer tools. GPT-4 (MATH algebra / TabMWP / GQA): TroVE 0.72/0.92/0.44 with 16/38/8 tools; CRAFT 0.68/0.88/0.45 with 282/181/525 tools; Creator 0.65/0.81/0.34. Trimming cut library size by 74 to 90% with a slight accuracy cost.
limits: Self-reported. A reanalysis (b22) found only 3 correct uses of a learned function in 3,201 test questions.
agent_relevance: A bigger library is not better; a library that only grows confuses the model.

source: Wang, Neubig, Fried (2024) TroVE: Inducing verifiable and efficient toolboxes
finding: Humans verified toolbox programs more accurately.
numbers: 6 evaluators, 100 WTQ examples. Detection accuracy up 13.0 to 14.3% with tool-based solutions; verification time cut by roughly 31 to 43% (figures read from garbled text, pairing unclear).
limits: Small human study; one dataset (WTQ).
agent_relevance: Short programs with named tools are easier for a checker or human to inspect.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Reuse of learned lemmas in LEGO-Prover was almost absent in the released logs.
numbers: Over 20,000 lemmas learned; 1,233 (6%) reached the prover's input. Exactly one lemma was reused verbatim, once. By name, no lemma appeared in 3 or more solutions. Problems solved per split: valid+GPT 127, valid+Human 135, test+GPT 111, test+Human 122.
quote: exactly one lemma is reused by the PROVER, and it is reused once
limits: Logs cover successful final attempts only. Soft reuse (copy and edit) was not measured here; see b25.
agent_relevance: The headline claim 'learns a reusable library' failed a direct check. Count reuse, not only accuracy.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Switching off cross-problem sharing in LEGO-Prover changed little.
numbers: Random 12-problem subset of miniF2F valid, 50 attempts, GPT-4o-mini, 2 trials: the ablation solved only 1 problem fewer than the full system.
limits: Tiny sample (12 problems). Original used GPT-3.5, now retired. Authors say the ablation was too aggressive, since it also removes the shared request store.
agent_relevance: Self-correction through the shared request store may explain the gain, not the library.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Re-running TroVE on MATH, learned functions were almost never used, and a no-library ablation did as well or better.
numbers: Reproduction within 2 points. Library held 15 functions, in 3 of 7 subjects. Only 2 functions were reused in a correct solution: is_perfect_square once, is_prime twice (3 successes in 3,201 test questions). No-reuse ablation (8 SKIP + 7 CREATE samples, 15 total) vs reproduced TroVE: count 0.250 vs 0.236, geometry 0.050 vs 0.058, intermediate algebra 0.134 vs 0.120, number 0.290 vs 0.258; 5 trials, significant on two splits.
quote: Typically, TroVE's library learning degrades its performance.
limits: CodeLlama-7B only; two datasets. The authors suspect MATH is not suited to function learning, since standard libraries cover shared parts.
agent_relevance: The gain came from 15 samples with a majority vote, not reuse. Equal-sample baselines are essential (G4, G7).

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2025) LLM library learning fails: a LEGO-Prover case study
finding: With three models and 3 trials, LEGO-Prover beat a draft-sketch-prove baseline at equal attempts for two models but lost with gpt-4o-mini.
numbers: miniF2F test, fixed attempts. gpt-4o-mini (100 attempts, full set): baseline 35.9 +/- 0.9 vs LEGO-Prover 25.8 +/- 1.6. gpt-4o (20% set, 50 attempts): 23.1 +/- 1.2 vs 29.3 +/- 3.1. o3-mini (10% set): 19.4 +/- 2.4 vs 27.8 +/- 4.8. Original claim: 45.5% (50% with human proofs) with GPT-3.5; replication nearer 38.5%.
limits: Subsets for costly models are small (about 25 to 50 problems), so rows are not comparable across columns.
agent_relevance: Result flips with the model: a library method can hurt in one setting.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2025) LLM library learning fails: a LEGO-Prover case study
finding: Per attempt, LEGO-Prover used about 6 to 14 times the compute of the baseline. At equal compute the baseline matched or won.
numbers: GPU budget ratio (cost proxy): gpt-4o-mini 5.84, gpt-4o 5.94, o3-mini 14.23. With attempts cut to match budget, the baseline was within 1 sd or better in every row. Extending the baseline to the same cost, it stayed within 1 sd or above LEGO-Prover throughout.
limits: Cost is a dollar proxy, not GPU time. Default is twice as many evolver as prover processes.
agent_relevance: Our G7: a scaffold that spends more must beat the plain model at the same tokens.

source: Berlot-Attwell, Rudzicz, Si (2025) LLM library learning fails: a LEGO-Prover case study
finding: Retrieved lemmas were copied in some solutions but were never reused across tasks, even softly.
numbers: Solutions containing a retrieved lemma verbatim / by name: gpt-4o 20% set 2/43 and 9/43; gpt-4o 10% 4/21 and 6/21; o3-mini 0/20 and 5/20; 4o-mini full 13/189 and 47/189. Cross-task reuse: 0 verbatim in all rows; 1 by name. Soft-reuse survival curves showed no gap between retrieved and non-retrieved lemmas.
limits: Soft use is measured by token edit distance, a fuzzy definition.
agent_relevance: The model uses a retrieved item as an example inside one task, but items are too task-specific to carry over.

source: Alford et al. (2021) Neural-guided, bidirectional program search for abstraction and reasoning
finding: On a 36-task symmetry subset of ARC, DreamCoder-style compression let the solver solve a few more tasks in the same time.
numbers: Five grid primitives, five rounds of enumerate and compress: 16 tasks at start, 17 after round one, 19 after round two, 22 at the end. Learned items include flip horizontally and stack horizontally.
limits: Tiny scale: 36 hand-picked tasks. The authors say DreamCoder's guidance is too weak for full ARC and switch to a different search.
agent_relevance: ARC is our honest control: library learning gave +6 of 36 on a hand-picked subset only. Do not expect it to transfer to all of ARC.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Adding an abstract-hypothesis step before writing the program raised GPT-4 accuracy on an ARC subset. This is abstraction without a stored library.
numbers: ARC subset, GPT-4: direct prompting 17%, abstract hypotheses 23%, plus LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%, plus human-selected hypotheses 33%. Without programs (language only) 19%. For 49 tasks with a selected hypothesis, 33 (67%) led to correct programs.
limits: Subset of ARC with small samples. Per-task abstraction, not a shared library.
agent_relevance: A per-task abstraction step may beat a stored library on ARC. Useful contrast.

source: Ahmed et al. (2026) Learning abstractions for hierarchical planning in program-synthesis agents (TheoryCoder-2)
finding: LLM-written abstractions reused across environments cut cost to zero for repeat tasks. Removing the curriculum or planner cost efficiency more than ability.
numbers: Minihack: after learning move_to in the 5x5 room, token use was 0 in the next three environments. BabyAI combine-skills level 1: 1,961 tokens vs 53,376 for a baseline. o4-mini at high effort took about 3 min on the Boss level.
limits: Text-based object states and a few games, one group. Authors say there is no systematic measure of abstraction quality; they compare with a hand-made oracle.
agent_relevance: Reuse pays when tasks share a skill and a runnable world model checks it.

source: Hernandez Cano et al. (2026) Prospective compression in human abstraction learning
finding: People built helpers that compress future tasks, not only past ones. DreamCoder-style retrospective compression and LLM synthesis did not match this when the task sequence changed over time.
numbers: N=60 on Prolific, 30 per experiment. Success 92.4% (E1), 81.9% (E2). Steps: people 3.93 vs raw-primitive program 8.64 (E1, t(13)=-3.72, p=0.0026, dz=-1.00); 4.51 vs 9.56 (E2, t(15)=-5.04, p=0.00015, dz=-1.26). 28/30 and 30/30 made at least one helper. In E2 human helpers compressed the corpus more than retrospective compression or LLM-based models.
limits: Preprint. Toy pattern-building task with 6 primitives. Models were run by the authors, one of them their own proposal.
agent_relevance: People keep solution depth flat by using helpers. Rank stored items by predicted future use, not only past use.

source: Tziafas and Kasaei (2024) Lifelong robot library learning (LRLL)
finding: A wake-sleep style LLM skill library for a simulated robot beat vanilla LLM and end-to-end baselines, with ablations of memory and abstraction.
numbers: I read the abstract and ablation setup but could not extract table values reliably from the two-column PDF; no figures recorded.
limits: Simulated tabletop. Numbers not confirmed. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as others: gains where reusable skills are clear.
